title: Where Your Poop Actually Goes After You Flush
summary: Follow one flush from the toilet through the lateral, the sewer main and the lift stations to the treatment plant, where screens, settling tanks and microbes clean the water before it goes back to a river. Plus what happens to the solids, and why heavy rain and wipes break the system.
tags: where does poop go when you flush
sources: NYC treatment: bar screens; primary settling tanks where the flow slows down and heavier sludge settles; air added so oxygen-loving microorganisms consume much of the organic material; final settling; disinfection with sodium hypochlorite, the same chemical found in household bleach; after about 8-10 hours the facilities release clean water; digesters heated to about 98°F for about 15 days, where microorganisms convert much of the material into biogas, which can produce heat and electricity for the facilities (NYC DEP, Wastewater Treatment System): https://www.nyc.gov/site/dep/water/wastewater-treatment-process.page

There are approximately 700 communities in the United States that have combined sewer systems, mostly in the northeast and around the Great Lakes (US EPA, Where Combined Sewer Overflows Are Located, updated 4 May 2026): https://www.epa.gov/npdes/where-combined-sewer-overflows-are-located

In a combined sewer system, wastewater and stormwater flow through the same pipes; in wet weather the combined flow can overwhelm the system, and permitted outfalls act as relief points that discharge untreated or partially treated stormwater and wastewater into nearby waterbodies (US EPA, Combined Sewer Overflow Basics): https://epa.gov/npdes/combined-sewer-overflow-basics

A sanitary sewer lateral runs from a building and slopes downward towards the street, typically 4, 5 or 6 inches in diameter for a single-family home; public sewer mains range from 8 to 36 inches in diameter; gravity moves most wastewater; lift stations pump wastewater to a gravity sewer where gravity alone won't work (City of Madison Engineering, How the Sanitary Sewer Works): https://www.cityofmadison.com/engineering/sanitary-sewer/education/how-the-sanitary-sewer-works

The sewer lateral connects the plumbing fixtures of a building (toilets, sinks, showers) to the sewer main (San Francisco Public Utilities Commission, How to take care of your sewer lateral): https://www.sfpuc.gov/about-us/news/how-take-care-your-sewer-lateral

New York City has 14 Wastewater Resource Recovery Facilities that together treat 1.3 billion gallons of wastewater daily; more than 6,000 miles of sewer pipes; 95 pumping stations (NYC DEP, Wastewater Resource Recovery Facilities): https://www.nyc.gov/site/dep/water/wastewater-treatment-plants.page

17,544 publicly owned treatment works served 270.4 million Americans, or 82 percent of the population, in 2022 (US EPA, 2022 Clean Watersheds Needs Survey Report to Congress, May 2024): https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2024-05/2022-cwns-report-to-congress.pdf

Screening removes large floating objects such as rags and sticks that might clog pipes or damage equipment; in a grit chamber cinders, sand and small stones settle; secondary (biological) treatment removes about 85 percent of the organic matter in sewage; done properly, chlorination kills more than 99 percent of the harmful bacteria in an effluent (US EPA, Wastewater Treatment Works... The Basics, EPA 833-F-98-002, May 1998): https://www3.epa.gov/npdes/pubs/bastre.pdf

Blue Plains treats close to 300 million gallons of wastewater a day (daily capacity 384 million gallons) and is the largest plant of its kind in the world (DC Water, Blue Plains Advanced Wastewater Treatment Plant): https://www.dcwater.com/about-dc-water/what-we-do/wastewater-treatment/blue-plains

Biosolids are sewage sludge treated to meet EPA Part 503 standards, intended for land application on agricultural land, forests, rangelands and other sites; in 2024 about 4 million dry metric tons of sewage sludge was reported, of which 59.5 percent was land applied and 14 percent incinerated (2024 Biosolids Annual Reports, about 2,350 reporting facilities only) (US EPA, Basic Information about Sewage Sludge and Biosolids): https://www.epa.gov/biosolids/basic-information-about-sewage-sludge-and-biosolids

In older cities, sewage and stormwater are often carried together in combined sewers; the Wastewater Systems Effluent Regulations set minimum effluent standards achievable through secondary treatment and address the largest point source of pollution in Canadian waters (ECCC, Overview of the Wastewater Systems Effluent Regulations): https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/wastewater/regulations.html

Over 2013-2023 about 86% of Canada's population was served by municipal wastewater systems; in 2023, 215 million m3 of municipal wastewater was discharged with no treatment, including 134 million m3 from combined sewer overflows (Environment and Climate Change Canada, Canadian Environmental Sustainability Indicators: Municipal wastewater treatment, Sept 2025): https://www.canada.ca/content/dam/eccc/documents/pdf/cesindicators/municipal-wastewater-treatmenet/2025/municipal-wastewater-treatment-en.pdf

Since the Anacostia River Tunnel was completed in March 2018, combined sewer overflows to the Anacostia River have been reduced by 90 percent; the tunnel delivers captured overflows to the Blue Plains plant, where they are treated before discharge to the Potomac (DC Water, Anacostia River Tunnel Project): https://www.dcwater.com/projects/anacostia-river-tunnel-project

The tunnel has a 23-foot inside diameter and can capture and hold up to 100 million gallons of combined sewage in heavy rainfalls (DC Water news release, 28 Mar 2018): https://www.dcwater.com/whats-going-on/news/dc-water-delivers-cleaner-anacostia-river-opening-first-leg-massive-tunnel

Accumulation of grease and debris causes 84 percent of sewer backups in New York City; DEP spends nearly $19 million annually to clean clogged sewers, dispose of wipes and repair damaged machinery (NYC DEP press release, 21 Feb 2019): https://www.nyc.gov/html/dep/html/press_releases/19-008pr.shtml

Every year Metro Vancouver and its members spend over $2 million dealing with wipes and other unflushables, which can bind with other materials to clog sewers; pee, poo and toilet paper are the only things that are safe to flush (Metro Vancouver, Wipes): https://metrovancouver.org/wipes

The US has more than 800,000 miles of public sewers (American Society of Civil Engineers, 2021 Report Card for America's Infrastructure: Wastewater): https://infrastructurereportcard.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/Wastewater-2021.pdf

scenes.narration: Flush. So where does your poop actually go? It just left on a trip, and that trip ends in a river.
In New York City, the trip takes about {8–10|eight to ten} hours. And what reaches the river is clean water.
Most of the time. In about {700|seven hundred} US communities, a hard rain can push some of it into the river untreated.
By the end, you'll know every stop, who does the dirty work, and how a storm, or a wipe, can break it.
Part one: the pipes.
Follow one flush. It drops out of your house, into a pipe called a lateral.
For a house, that pipe is usually {4–6 in|four to six inches} across, and it slopes down toward the street.
Under the street, it joins the sewer main, a public pipe your neighbors share.
What keeps it moving? Mostly gravity. The pipes slope downhill, so the flow just follows.
Where the land climbs, a lift station pumps it back up, and gravity takes over again.
New York City alone has {95|ninety-five} pumping stations, and more than {6,000|six thousand} miles of sewer pipe.
If you like knowing where things really go, subscribe. There's a new system every other day.
Part two: the plant.
All those pipes end at a treatment plant. The US has more than {17,500|seventeen and a half thousand} of them.
Step one: screens. Metal bars catch rags and sticks. Then sand and grit sink out.
Step two: settling. In big tanks, the flow slows down, and heavier solids sink to the bottom.
Step three: air gets pumped in, and microbes eat the organic matter. Your poop becomes their lunch.
This biological step removes about {85%|eighty-five percent} of the organic matter in sewage.
Step four: disinfection. New York uses sodium hypochlorite, the same chemical found in household bleach.
Done properly, chlorine kills more than {99%|ninety-nine percent} of the harmful bacteria.
Then the clean water goes out, into a river, a lake or the ocean. That's the river from the start.
Washington's Blue Plains plant cleans close to {300 million|three hundred million} gallons a day, then sends it into the Potomac.
The solids that sank go to digesters, heated to about {98°F|ninety-eight degrees}. In about {15|fifteen} days, microbes turn much of it into biogas.
What's left becomes biosolids. In {2024|twenty twenty-four}, {59.5%|fifty-nine and a half percent} of reported sludge was spread on land, like farm fields.
Part three: rain and wipes.
Now, the rain. In older cities, sewage and storm water share the same pipes.
In a hard rain, that flow can overwhelm the system. So relief outlets spill the mix, untreated or partly treated, into a river.
Canada reported {134 million|a hundred thirty-four million} cubic metres of overflow in {2023|twenty twenty-three}.
DC's fix: a tunnel that holds up to {100 million|a hundred million} gallons of overflow. Since {2018|twenty eighteen}, overflows into the Anacostia are down {90%|ninety percent}.
The other trouble starts at home: wipes and grease. Wipes bind with other stuff and clog sewers.
In New York, grease and debris caused {84%|eighty-four percent} of sewer backups, the city said in {2019|twenty nineteen}.
Metro Vancouver spends over {$2 million|two million dollars} a year on wipes. Its rule: pee, poo and toilet paper. That's it.
So that's one flush: lateral, main, pumps, screens, tanks, microbes, bleach, river. {8–10|Eight to ten} hours, unless it rains, or somebody flushes a wipe.
Next up: what really happens to your recycling. Pick a pipe.
